issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may not replace a possible finding of the appellate court with its own view merely because it would assess the evidence differently.
material_facts: The appellate rent court considered the partnership deeds and other evidence and found that the tenant was a genuine partner in the business using the premises, so there was no subletting.
The High Court, exercising revision, reappraised the same evidence and reversed that finding, treating the partnership as a camouflage.
The appellate court’s view was supported by evidence and was not impossible or perverse.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction by substituting its view for the possible view reached by the appellate court.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 29(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, revision is distinct from appeal and does not permit rehearing on the facts or substitution of one possible view for another. The revisional court must ensure that the law was correctly applied, material facts were properly appreciated, and the decision does not produce a miscarriage of justice. The Court relied on Hari Shankar v. Rao Girdhari Lal Chowdhury, Puranchand v. Motilal, Krishnawati v. Hans Raj, Phiroze Bamanji Desai v. Chandrakant M. Patel, and Bhai Chand Ratanshi v. Laxmishankar Tribhavan; it declined to follow the broader approach to revision in M/s Kasturbhai Ramchand Panchal & Brothers v. Firm of Mohanlal Nathubhai and referred to Punamchandra Revashankar Joshi v. Ramjibhai Maganlal.

rule.if: rent_control_revision and appellate_finding_supported and revisional_court_reappraised_evidence and no_perversity_or_impossibility

predicates.rent_control_revision: The proceeding is a revision from an appellate decision in a rent-control matter.
predicates.appellate_finding_supported: The appellate court made a finding supported by its consideration of the evidence.
predicates.revisional_court_reappraised_evidence: The revisional court reassessed the evidence and substituted its own view for the appellate court’s view.
predicates.no_perversity_or_impossibility: The appellate court’s finding was neither perverse nor an impossible view of the evidence.

issues.definition: When a rent-control revision challenges a supported appellate finding that is neither perverse nor impossible, reassessing the evidence does not permit the revisional court to substitute its own view.

issues.legal_issue: An arrangement may constitute a genuine partnership even when a partner receives a fixed or limited share of profits, does not share losses, and lacks authority to operate the firm’s bank accounts.
material_facts: The tenant joined the business through partnership deeds that provided for a share of profits and made him an agent for certain limited purposes.
The tenant contributed the tenancy of the premises for use by the business.

The deeds provided that the tenant would not share losses, would receive a minimum amount, and would not operate the bank accounts; the Court found nothing inherently illegal or improper in those terms.

Registrations, licences, tax records, and evidence that the deeds were acted upon supported the existence of the partnership; no partner claimed in the dissolution proceedings that the deeds were fictitious.
The appellate court considered the relevant principles and evidence and found a genuine partnership.
issues.conclusion: The evidence permitted the finding that a genuine partnership existed; the terms limiting the tenant’s profit share, excluding loss-sharing, or restricting bank access did not by themselves disprove it.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 6 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 require attention to the real relationship shown by all relevant facts. Partnership requires an agreement among the persons concerned, an agreement to share business profits, and a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all; agency is essential, while sharing profits and contributing to losses are not alone decisive. Whether a partnership exists is a mixed question of law and fact. The Court relied on Chimanram Motilal v. Jayantilal Chhaganlal and Mohammed Musa Sahib v. N.K. Mohammed Ghouse Sahib.

rule.if: partnership_status_dispute and partnership_agreement and profit_sharing and business_carried_on_for_all and agency_for_firm

predicates.partnership_status_dispute: The dispute concerns whether persons carrying on a business have a partnership relationship.
predicates.partnership_agreement: The persons concerned agreed to carry on the business in partnership.
predicates.profit_sharing: The agreement provides for sharing profits from the business.
predicates.business_carried_on_for_all: The business is carried on by all or some of the persons concerned for their common business arrangement.
predicates.agency_for_firm: A person carrying on the business acts as an agent for the others or for the firm.

issues.definition: A genuine partnership is possible where persons in a partnership-status dispute agreed to share business profits and the business is carried on by one or more of them acting for all.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s permission for a partnership firm to use leased premises does not amount to subletting if the tenant remains in legal possession.
material_facts: The business operating in the premises was a partnership in which the tenant was a partner.
The tenant contributed the tenancy of the premises for use by the partnership and retained legal possession.
The other partners’ use of the premises was for the partnership business.
issues.conclusion: There was no subletting merely because the partnership firm used the premises while the tenant retained legal possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 13(1)(e) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, subletting requires the tenant to part with legal possession; another person’s use of the premises is insufficient if the tenant retains that possession. The Court relied on Madras Bangalore Transport Co. (West) v. Inder Singh, Mehta Jagjivan Vanechand v. Doshi Vanechand Harakhchand, and Gundalapalli Rangamannar Chetty v. Desu Rangiah.

rule.if: eviction_subletting_proceeding and tenant_is_partner and partnership_uses_premises and tenant_retains_legal_possession

predicates.eviction_subletting_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground that the tenant sublet the premises.
predicates.tenant_is_partner: The tenant is a partner in the business using the premises.
predicates.partnership_uses_premises: The partnership business uses the leased premises.
predicates.tenant_retains_legal_possession: The tenant has not parted with legal possession of the premises.

issues.definition: When a tenant who is a partner retains legal possession while the partnership uses the premises, that use is not subletting in an eviction proceeding based on subletting.
